title: Divide Array Into Increasing Sequences
statement:
The array `nums` is sorted in non-decreasing order. Decide whether its elements can be split into one or more disjoint subsequences so that:

- every element of `nums` belongs to exactly one subsequence,
- each subsequence is strictly increasing, and
- each subsequence has at least `k` elements.

Return `true` when such a split exists and `false` otherwise.
constraints: nums is sorted in non-decreasing order
notes:
## Intuition

Searching over every way to split the array is exponential. The key observation is that equal values can never share a subsequence, because each subsequence must strictly increase. So if some value appears `maxFreq` times, at least `maxFreq` subsequences are needed, and since each needs `k` elements, `maxFreq * k` elements are required in total.

That condition is also enough. If `maxFreq * k <= n`, make exactly `maxFreq` subsequences and deal the sorted array into them in turn (index `i` goes to subsequence `i mod maxFreq`). Copies of one value sit in a block of at most `maxFreq` consecutive positions, so they land in different subsequences; elements `maxFreq` apart are therefore strictly increasing; and each subsequence receives at least `floor(n / maxFreq) >= k` elements.

## Approach

1. Because `nums` is sorted, equal values form consecutive runs. Walk the array keeping `run`, the length of the current run.
2. When `nums[i]` equals the previous value, extend `run`; otherwise start a new run of length 1.
3. Track the longest run in `maxFreq`.
4. Return whether `maxFreq * k <= nums.length`.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums = [1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4, 4]`, `k = 3`. The runs are `1` (length 1), `2, 2`, `3, 3` and `4, 4` (length 2 each), so `maxFreq = 2`. Two subsequences of at least 3 elements need 6 elements and we have 7, so the answer is `true`: for example `[1, 2, 3, 4]` and `[2, 3, 4]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): one pass over the sorted array.
- Space: O(1): only two counters.

## Pitfalls

- The subsequences must be strictly increasing, so duplicates force extra subsequences; the answer depends on the largest count, not on the number of distinct values.
- Every element must be used. Leaving the extra copies out is not allowed.
- No sorting or hash map is needed: the input is already sorted, so counting runs is enough.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `run` | length of the block of equal values ending at `i` |
| `maxFreq` | largest number of copies of any value, the minimum number of subsequences |
| `i` | current index in `nums` |

narration.2: maxFreq will hold the largest number of copies of any single value.
narration.3: run is the length of the current block of equal values.
narration.5: Walk through the sorted array once.
narration.6: Sorted input keeps equal values together, so compare with the previous element.
narration.7: Same value as before: the current block grows.
narration.9: A new value starts a fresh block of length one.
narration.11: Keep the longest block seen so far.
narration.14: maxFreq subsequences are needed, each with k elements; the split works exactly when that many elements exist.
